outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 bears on whether there are infinitely many Wilson primes: the only known ones are still 5, 13 and 563, the largest published search (all primes below 2×10¹³, arXiv 2012, Math. Comp. 2014) found no new ones, and the 2024–2026 papers I found concern Wilson quotients or neighbouring congruences, not the set of Wilson primes.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many Wilson primes, i.e. infinitely many primes p with (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p²), equivalently p² divides (p−1)!+1. The statement names no constant, range or parts; the definition used is the standard one, which the statement presupposes. Not asked by the bullet: the heuristic count of Wilson primes in an interval, generalised Wilson primes of order n, and function-field analogues.

events.delivers: Identifies 13 as a Wilson prime. One instance; finitely many instances of a question about infinitely many primes move nothing toward infinitude.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many Wilson primes exist (all of problem_asks).

events.what_happened: Costa, Gerbicz and Harvey, 'A search for Wilson primes', arXiv:1209.3436 (submitted 15 Sep 2012; v3 5 Dec 2012), published Math. Comp. 83 (290), 3071–3091 (2014). They searched all primes p < 2×10¹³ for (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p²) and state: 'We found no new Wilson primes up to this bound.' They also give the first known algorithm computing (p−1)! mod p² in average polynomial time per prime. The search is described as consuming over 1.1 million CPU hours, with a separate 440,000-hour verification run.
events.revisions: v1 15 Sep 2012; v3 5 Dec 2012 (arXiv abstract page); journal version Math. Comp. 83 (2014), 3071–3091.
events.delivers: Establishes that, among all primes below 2×10¹³, only 5, 13 and 563 satisfy the congruence (no further Wilson primes in that range). Restricted to a finite range: it says any further Wilson prime exceeds 2×10¹³ and says nothing about whether there are infinitely many.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many Wilson primes exist (all of problem_asks). The search covers a finite initial range only.

summary: The question is whether there are infinitely many primes p with (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p²). Wikipedia (fetched; footer reports last edit 21 Aug 2026), the OEIS entry A007540 (fetched; last modified 11 Oct 2026 per the fetch) and the PrimePages glossary (search snippet) all still list only 5, 13 and 563 and still call the question open, with a heuristic expectation of infinitely many. The largest published search is Costa, Gerbicz and Harvey (arXiv 1209.3436, 15 Sep 2012; Math. Comp. 83 (2014), 3071–3091): I opened the arXiv abstract and the ar5iv HTML and quote its statement 'We found no new Wilson primes up to this bound' for all primes below 2×10¹³. Nothing I found since 26 January 2024 changes this. The in-window papers I opened concern Wilson quotients or neighbouring congruences and do not mention Wilson primes: Kellner Parts I (HTML full text), II and III (abstracts), Morozov 2505.16201 (abstract), Matsuno 2607.10106 (abstract, resolving two Kellner conjectures), and Howard 2604.09714 (abstract). OEIS cites arXiv 2604.01578 (Matsusaka, Miyazaki, Yara), but that paper concerns finite Dobiński/Euler analogues and I could not establish why OEIS cites it. Nothing relevant to the infinitude question is in a published or preprint form after 2024 that I could find; the 2026 AI-tracker results I checked did not include this problem. Close calls: (a) a reader could treat Kellner/Matsuno's congruences as bearing on the Wilson prime condition, since (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p²) is W_p ≡ 0 (mod p); I judge they change no instance count and no infinitude statement, but the call is for the later pass. (b) The function-field results (Thakur 2013 and 2022/2024; Sauerberg–Shu–Thakur–Todd 2013) show infinitude holds for F_q[t] for many q and are explicitly analogues; I record them as different questions. (c) Thakur's 2024 JTNB paper is published in the window, but its first public argument is the November 2022 arXiv preprint, so it is dated 2022; its claim that the integer question remains open appears only in a search snippet, which I could not confirm in the text. The historical events (1892, 1913, 1930, 1953, 1997, 1994, 2006/2008, 2012/2014) are all finite searches or single instances and move nothing toward infinitude; I record them because the instruction is to record every event. Pre-window items the search turned up but that are not events: a 2018 Ordowski–Resta conjectured characterisation of Wilson primes via power sums (OEIS A007540, a conjecture only), and an unresolved claim from a search snippet that arXiv 1802.01909 (Hussein, 2018) contains a conjecture on (n−1)! ≡ −1 (mod n³); the abstract I opened does not mention it. The AI search found no AI system credited with any Wilson-prime result: the Astra batch of ten results from OpenAI (1 Aug 2026; GitHub README opened) contains no Wilson or prime-congruence result; no press or lab announcement or tracker names this problem; the Epoch FrontierMath Open Problems list could not be read in full.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a larger in-window event: Kellner Parts I–III and Matsuno (2607.10106) work on W_p = ((p−1)!+1)/p modulo higher prime powers, and the Wilson prime condition is exactly W_p ≡ 0 (mod p). A reader could argue these results sharpen the Wilson-prime condition and so move a quantity the bullet is about. On the scope test they do not: they describe congruences for W_p mod p^k, give no new Wilson prime and no bound, and say nothing about whether the set of such primes is infinite. The strongest case for a larger historical event is Costa–Gerbicz–Harvey, whose result is a computation-scale bound that a reader could see as the 'quantity' of Wilson primes below a bound moving from 5×10⁸ to 2×10¹³. That is a finite census of a universal existential question, and does not change infinitude.
what_would_settle_it: For infinitude: a proof or a construction of infinitely many p with p² | (p−1)!+1, which no source I found contains. For the search status: a published or preprint extension of the search past 2×10¹³ (not infinitude, but would move the bound); the Ibercivis and GIMPS Wilson prime project status pages; the AMS record of Costa et al. (403 on fetch); the Crandall–Dilcher–Pomerance 1997 PDF, the Sauerberg et al. PDF and the Thakur 2013 article, to confirm their statements about the integer question; and the full text of Kellner Parts II and III, Morozov, Matsuno and Howard to confirm they do not discuss Wilson primes or AI involvement.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many Wilson primes exist. Every historical event is a single instance or a finite search (instances, F5), including Costa–Gerbicz–Harvey to 2×10¹³; finding 563 is an instance, not a witness to infinitude, so object_role is null. The function-field results of Thakur and Sauerberg–Shu–Thakur–Todd answer the F_q[t] analogue (variant). The 2025–2026 papers by Morozov, Kellner, Matsuno and Howard settle questions about Wilson-quotient congruences modulo higher prime powers, which are different questions, so they are variant rather than bearing on the set of Wilson primes; Matsusaka et al. does not bear on the problem at all (none). No AI involvement in any event.
judgement.doubts: Kellner/Matsuno-type congruences could be read as 'none' (bearing without settling) rather than 'variant'; both are discarded identically. Thakur 2013 and Sauerberg et al. were verified only via journal listings and snippets.
